summary: Describes how to carry IP datagrams, and the higher-level protocols above them, over Network Systems Corporation's HYPERchannel equipment. It targets network planners and implementors who already know TCP/IP, and includes an appendix reviewing HYPERchannel technology. It was an Internet standard and was later updated by RFC 5494.

plainLanguage.summary: HYPERchannel was a fast network built from adapters joined by coaxial cables, and it had no agreed way of carrying IP. This RFC says where the IP datagram sits inside a HYPERchannel message, how a host finds the HYPERchannel address that belongs to an IP address, and how the older 16-bit form and the newer 32-bit form differ.

subtitle: How to carry IP datagrams, and an ARP variant, over Network Systems Corporation's HYPERchannel equipment.

tldr.problem: The Internet Protocol had to be carried over HYPERchannel, a high-speed network made of coaxial trunks and adapters, and the way IP did not fit on it was settled by habit rather than by agreement.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the HYPERchannel network message in two forms, a 16-bit and a 32-bit one, and says where an IP datagram goes inside each: at an offset the header names, with the rest of the datagram in the associated data block that follows.
tldr.outcome: The document made the existing practice official and defined an ARP for HYPERchannel and a registry of protocol type numbers, and it was later updated by RFC 5494.

today: RFC 1044 was an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted, though it was later updated by RFC 5494. It describes how to carry IP over Network Systems Corporation's HYPERchannel equipment, and it is aimed at network planners and implementors who already know the TCP/IP protocol suite.

sections.title: Goals of the Document
sections.content:
The document has four aims. The first is to bless a de facto standard for IP over HYPERchannel, which had already been implemented by Tektronix, Cray, NASA Ames and others, and to resolve the interoperability problems that remained in it so that as few changes as possible were needed to existing software.

The second is to introduce the extension to 32-bit addressing. The newer Network Systems Corporation products were moving from the 16-bit TO address, because the original scheme could only reach 256 adapter boxes and 40 or so adapters had been considered a large network. The document introduces the extension to the user community and says how IP datagrams work in the new mode.

The third is to define an Address Resolution Protocol for HYPERchannel and other NSC products. The RFC notes that existing products do not support the broadcast modes that make ARP useful, while many organizations had expressed interest in ARP servers at a known network address, so a host driver that could generate and recognise this ARP protocol could be ready when the pieces arrived.

The fourth is to standardize the unofficial message type field that reserves byte 8 of the HYPERchannel network message, so that NSC could run a network protocol registry in which any interested party could obtain a unique value for its own protocol, with the assigned numbers and their owners published periodically.
sections.plainLanguage: The document was written to settle four practical questions: what a standard way of running IP over HYPERchannel looks like, how the newer larger addressing works, how a host finds the hardware address that goes with an IP address, and what the byte that says what kind of message this is should contain.

sections.title: The HYPERchannel Network Message
sections.content:
A HYPERchannel network message has two parts. The Message Proper is a header of up to 64 bytes, and its first 10 bytes hold what the network adapters need to deliver the message. The Associated Data is an optional second part of unlimited length when the message travels over HYPERchannel A trunks, while other equipment, such as HYPERchannel B or a local A400 adapter, limits it to 4K bytes. If the information fits inside the Message Proper, no associated data is sent at all.

The two parts are treated quite differently by the link protocols. A message with no associated data is sent using abbreviated protocols and can be queued in the receiving network adapter, which keeps the elapsed time for sending and receiving short. When associated data is present, the HYPERchannel A adapters give up logical resources towards driving the host interface and the coaxial trunks.

In the basic 16-bit form, byte 0 holds two four-bit masks saying which of the four possible coaxial trunks to use for the message and for the reply, and byte 1 holds three flags: Associated Data Present, Burst Mode, which dedicates a single trunk for the duration of the message, and Exception, which tells some channel-programmed host interfaces that the message is out of band and needs special handling. Bytes 4 and 5 hold the TO address, the physical address of the destination adapter plus a port number, and bytes 6 and 7 the FROM address. The FROM address is not used during transmission; it is passed to the receiving host so that a response can be returned to the point of origin.

The newer 32-bit form replaces the single 16-bit TO address with four fields: a TO domain number, a TO network number, a 24-bit physical adapter address and a port number, with the high-order bit of the adapter address reserved as an outnet bit. A local collection of adapters connected by coax or fibre is one network, and each network can have up to 256 directly addressable adapters. A large NSC network can have up to 64K networks, which is why the 16-bit network field was divided into a network number and a domain number. Bridges decide whether to forward a message by examining all 24 bits in bytes 2 to 5 of the header, using masks for the domain numbers, network numbers and local addresses they should accept.
sections.plainLanguage: Each HYPERchannel message has a small header, up to 64 bytes, and optionally a large block of data after it. The header says where the message is going and how it should travel, which is why a bridge can forward it without reading the data itself.

sections.title: IP Inside the 16-Bit Message
sections.content:
With the basic 16-bit header, byte 8 carries the value 5 to say that the message carries IP traffic, and no other well-behaved protocol using HYPERchannel should use that value. Byte 9 holds the offset to the start of the IP header within the message proper. Bytes 10 and 11 hold an IP type designator of 0x34, a value earlier implementors had chosen for reasons now of only historical interest, and the offset to the start of the IP header measured from byte 12. That second offset is the one a receiver must respect, and its maximum permissible value is 52, which puts the start of the IP header at the beginning of the associated data block.

The IP datagram is treated as one contiguous block of data that flows from byte 63 of the message proper into the first byte of associated data. If the datagram fits inside the message proper, only the message proper is transmitted, and its length should always be 64 bytes even when the datagram and the HYPERchannel header do not fill all 64 of them. If the datagram spills over into the associated data, both the message and the data are sent. The length of the associated data received should not be used as a guide to the length of the IP datagram, because some machines cannot send a length of data that is an exact number of bytes; the length has to be taken from the IP header instead. A driver should check that the associated data received is at least long enough to hold the whole datagram.
sections.plainLanguage: In the older, 16-bit form, the IP datagram is placed in the message at an offset that the header states, and any part of the datagram that does not fit continues in the associated data block. The receiver works out the length of the datagram from the IP header rather than from how much data arrived.

sections.title: The 32-Bit Message and Its New Flags
sections.content:
With 32-bit addressing the header is longer. Byte 8 again carries a message type, this time the value 6, so a receiver can tell the two forms apart; for the sake of older drivers a zero in byte 8 is treated as a 16-bit message. The offset to the start of the IP header is in byte 9, and valid offsets run from 16 to 44 bytes inclusive. The limit of 44 is imposed so that routing decisions on the vast majority of IP datagrams can be made by examining only the message proper, since a basic IP datagram still fits there if it begins at offset 44.

Three new flag bits have been defined. The CRC bit marks a 32-bit checksum that the newer host adapters can generate for the entire network message; it is appended to the end of the associated data block and preserved through the whole delivery process until it is checked and removed by the adapter that is the ultimate recipient, giving end-to-end assurance that data has moved correctly through intermediate networks and adapter hardware. The SRC bit says the 32-bit FROM address in the message really is where the message came from; any intermediate adapter may turn the bit off if the FROM address is not a TO address that would receive the message if it were going the opposite way, so a host that receives the message with the bit still set knows the address can be trusted. The GNA bit says that 32-bit addressing is present in the message, in which case bytes 2 and 3 should also be non-zero.

The message also carries an age count, which serves the same purpose as the IP time to live: each time a 32-bit message passes through a bridge the count is decremented by one, and the bridge discards the message when the result is zero. Two offset fields, the next header offset and the header end offset, both hold the value 16 when unused, which says both that there are no extra TO addresses and that the user protocol begins at byte 16. They exist so that loose source routing, a list of TO addresses that fixes the path of a message through the network, could be expressed, although the RFC does not consider that capability worth building into IP over HYPERchannel.
sections.plainLanguage: The newer, larger form of the header adds a few flags: a checksum of the whole message, a flag saying the sender's address is right, and a counter that stops a message from circling the network forever.

sections.title: Interoperating with Existing Implementations
sections.content:
The basic format described in the RFC is a compromise between several implementations of IP over HYPERchannel, and not all of them interoperate. Two families of driver were known to exist.

The first was the Cray-NASA Ames protocol. It was in the widest production use and had the largest number of supported drivers, and it is identical with the standard described in the RFC with the sole exception that those drivers set bytes 8 and 9 to zero. Those bytes were ignored by most implementations of this driver, so they were given values here to formalize the use of the message type field and to make it consistent with the 32-bit protocol.

The second was the Tektronix-Berkeley protocol, historically the first implementation, developed at Tektronix and later carried to Berkeley and BSD UNIX. It differs in several ways. Bytes 8 through 11 are always zero, and the IP header always starts on byte 12; comments in some of these drivers call byte 11 an IP header offset, but apparently that value is never processed. Its packaging of the datagram is the real incompatibility, a consequence of historical difficulties with sending and receiving very small blocks of associated data on VAX machines. If the entire IP datagram is 54 bytes or less, it fits in the 64-byte message proper, no associated data is sent, and the message proper is transmitted at the exact length needed to enclose the datagram with no padding. If the IP header is longer than 54 bytes, all the higher level protocol information, such as the TCP or UDP header and their associated data fields, is placed in the associated data block with the TCP or UDP header beginning at the start of it, and the message proper is sent at the length of the HYPERchannel header plus the IP header rather than padded out to 64 bytes.

The RFC follows the Cray-Ames approach for three reasons: Cray Research had done exemplary work in bringing IP over HYPERchannel to other hosts, so four or five vendor-supported implementations used it; the two-part structure lets a machine make protocol decisions before staging the transfer of an immense block of associated data into memory, which many network coprocessors and intelligent I/O subsystems prefer; and some TCP users, mostly secure Department of Defense sites, intended to load IP datagrams with optional fields in the future, which the Tektronix-Berkeley implementation cannot handle when the IP header length exceeds 54 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Two incompatible families of driver existed when the RFC was written. The document settles on one of them, the one already in widest use, so that machines from different vendors could talk to each other.

sections.title: Finding the Address to Put in the Header
sections.content:
To send an IP datagram, the driver has to turn the destination IP address into the HYPERchannel address that goes in the header. The RFC describes four techniques.

The first is truncation, where the low order 16 bits of the IP address are used as the HYPERchannel address, which more or less treats the set of HYPERchannel boxes as a Class B IP network. It is simple and needs no configuration files, but the RFC discourages its long-term use: it cannot work with a Class C address, where the physical TO address is not controllable, or with a Class A address, where host addresses are carefully administered; it does not support subnetworks; and it is quite incompatible with 32-bit HYPERchannel addresses. Decoupling the two addresses also gives a site more flexibility, because the IP address becomes logical and can move around a site with the host while the HYPERchannel address keeps its physical character and identifies where the equipment sits.

The second is local resolution through configuration files. The driver looks the IP address up in a generally hashed table, and the entry holds the first 6 bytes of the HYPERchannel header used to reach the next IP node. Because implementations such as the 4.3BSD UNIX IP also give their lower level drivers the IP address of the next gateway, the table only has to contain the IP hosts and gateway addresses directly accessible on the HYPERchannel, which keeps it manageable. Each line of the file has the form <type> <hostname> <trunks/flags> <domain/net> <addr> <MTU>. The types are host, ahost for an additional interface to the same host, loop for a loopback entry, address and arpserver. The MTU field gives the largest IP datagram the destination is prepared to receive, and if it is absent a value of 4148 is assumed. An arpserver entry names a server to ask for address resolution, and the servers are tried in turn until one answers.

The third is an ARP server, reached simply by putting the server's address in the TO address of the message. ARP servers only listen for messages that arrive on their well-known normal address and do not respond to ARP broadcasts, though properly equipped IP drivers should respond to broadcasts when they appear. A server that receives a message containing an address it cannot resolve ignores it, so that another server may be tried at the source's next attempt. When the address is resolvable the server places the known HYPERchannel address and MTU size in the response and returns it to the location in the FROM address. Unlike broadcast ARP, the server is called upon twice when two hosts that do not yet know each other try to reach one another, because the destination never saw the request and must contact the server itself when its higher level protocols first generate a datagram.

The fourth is broadcast ARP, which becomes possible when the equipment supports broadcast. A driver configured for it emits the ARP message on a broadcast instead of to a well-known address, and drivers on other hosts listen on the broadcast address for ARP. The processing otherwise follows RFC-826: messages are answered if and only if the destination IP driver is authoritative for the designated IP address, and whenever an ARP message is processed the driver takes the source HYPERchannel address and MTU size and adds them to its address resolution tables. A static entry from the configuration file wins over dynamic ARP information, on the premise that the only useful purpose of static routing in a broadcast ARP environment is to add authentication, since it is easy to lie with ARP.
sections.plainLanguage: To send a packet, the driver has to know which HYPERchannel address to put in the header for the destination IP address. The RFC describes four ways of working that out, from copying part of the IP address, through a list kept on each host, to asking a server, to asking every host on the network at once.

sections.title: The ARP Message and the Size Agreement
sections.content:
The HYPERchannel ARP message reuses the layout of the Ethernet protocol with a few differences. It travels in the 32-bit message form, and the 16-bit message type value 0x0700 is reserved for the exclusive use of ARP. The ARP hardware type for HYPERchannel is 8. The HYPERchannel protocol type field, which on Ethernet distinguishes IP from other protocols that need address resolution, is identical to bytes 8 and 9 of a 32-bit message carrying IP, which is 0x0600. The HYPERchannel address length is 6, enough to hold the four-byte HYPERchannel address and two bytes for the largest IP datagram that the source and destination can handle.

Those two bytes carry the size agreement. The field is the maximum size of the IP header plus data that the sender is prepared to receive, and it does not include the HYPERchannel hardware header or any offset between the header and the start of the IP datagram. Transmitting drivers should send the minimum of the source and destination sizes negotiated at ARP time. The maximum is 65536, the largest IP datagram then current, and the offset length is left out so that the value fits in a 16-bit field. The RFC works through two examples. A typical 16-bit packet has a 12-byte hardware header, a 12-byte offset, a 40-byte IP and TCP header and 4096 bytes of data, which gives an MTU of 4136. A typical 32-bit packet has a 16-byte hardware header, an 8-byte offset, the same 40-byte IP and TCP header and 4096 bytes of associated data, which also gives an MTU of 4136. The offsets are chosen so that user data starts page-aligned, which the RFC calls an implementation decision that can be modified as required.
sections.plainLanguage: The ARP message is the Ethernet one with the pieces renamed. It also carries a number: the largest IP datagram the sender can take. Two hosts that can reach each other then use the smaller of the two sizes, so that neither is sent something too big.

sections.title: Integrity and Source Checking
sections.content:
This document has no security section of its own, but it does describe three mechanisms that bear on integrity. The CRC flag lets the newer host adapters compute a 32-bit checksum for the entire network message as soon as it is received from the host, append it to the end of the associated data block, and preserve it through delivery until the adapter that is the ultimate recipient checks it and removes it, which gives a high degree of assurance that data has been moved correctly through all the intermediate networks and adapter hardware. The SRC flag lets a sender assert that the FROM address in the header really is where the message came from, and any intermediate adapter involved in the delivery may turn the bit off if the FROM address is not a TO address that would receive the message if it were travelling the opposite way. The RFC notes that, by paying careful attention to the physical security of the adapters and the intermediate links between networks, a high degree of security can be built into systems that simply examine the FROM address of a message to decide whether the request it carries is legitimate.

On address resolution, the RFC says that ARP information which contradicts a static entry should be ignored, on the premise that the only useful purpose of static routing in a broadcast ARP environment is to add authentication, as it is easy to lie with ARP.
sections.plainLanguage: The document has no section on security, but it does say how to check that a message has not been damaged and that it really came from the address it claims. It also warns that anyone on the network can answer an address request with a false address, which is why a host's own configured list should win.
